examples.title: Win the argument or be heard
examples.scenario: A heated dispute is escalating in the Monday standoff, and the upset employee keeps repeating herself. Magdalena Ruiz, the team lead, feels the urge to jump in and prove her own point. She recalls that most conflict eases once a person feels genuinely heard, the way a tense disagreement with chef Daniel Humm cooled once both sides felt understood. Before the meeting boils over, Magdalena has to decide whether to win the argument or first make the other person feel fully understood.
examples.whatToDo: Before pushing your own point, make the other person feel genuinely heard, because most conflict eases once someone feels understood, and people want that more than they want agreement.

examples.title: The same blunt feedback for all
examples.scenario: 'I deliver the same blunt feedback to everyone, that is just being fair,' the manager said. Bertrand Shaw, an executive coach, disagreed. 'The same message has to be packaged differently per person; some need direct intensity, others a gentler word. Even Daniel Humm got feedback tuned to how he received it.' He pointed at her notes. 'Before your next review, you have to decide how each person actually prefers to receive a hard truth.'
examples.whatToDo: Tune how you deliver correction to how each person best receives it, because the same blunt script for everyone is not fairness; it is feedback that simply fails to land.

examples.title: A winner or a third option
examples.scenario: Ngozi Eze is the product lead, deadlocked with a peer over a design decision while the meeting wants a winner. She could push to win and leave him resentful, or reject the win-or-lose frame and hunt for a third option both can accept, the way a design standoff with Daniel Humm was settled by inventing a custom solution instead of one side conceding. The clock is ticking. Before the decision locks, Ngozi has to choose between winning the argument and inventing a solution that satisfies them both.
examples.whatToDo: When two people deadlock, reject the win-or-lose choice and invent a creative third solution both can accept, because a settlement both own beats a declared winner and a resentful loser.

examples.title: Correction without the praise
examples.scenario: Before, Soren Dahl ran his team on relentless correction and almost no praise, and his best people slowly disengaged. After Soren, the operations manager, flipped the ratio and made praise his primary lever, given in public, the mood and the output both lifted, an approach leaders beside Daniel Humm modeled by treating praise as affirmation and criticism as investment. He still corrected, privately and without heat. A year later people brought him problems early, because praise had made the criticism feel like investment.
examples.whatToDo: Track your praise-to-correction ratio for a week, then deliberately tip it toward public praise, because criticism only lands as investment once a person already feels valued.

examples.title: When feedback went silent
examples.scenario: Feedback had dried up, so the department director Yara Najjar reviewed the quarter Monday. Every time someone raised a concern, she had gotten defensive, explained it away, or bristled. Reading the silence, Yara saw the cost: by reacting badly to criticism, she had taught her team to stop bringing it, the discipline leaders around Daniel Humm protected by staying genuinely receptive. Now she heard nothing, and the real problems surfaced far too late.
examples.whatToDo: Stay genuinely receptive when criticized instead of defensive, because reacting badly teaches people to stop bringing you feedback, and then the real problems reach you too late to fix.

examples.title: Setting a feedback norm
examples.scenario: Two weeks before the team's big launch, the people lead Conrad Pike must decide on a feedback norm. One option lets correction happen however and whenever, even publicly in the heat of the moment. The other makes correction private, calm, and aimed at behavior, with disputes resolved before anyone leaves for the night, the disciplines leaders alongside Daniel Humm kept. The team is conflict-averse. Conrad weighs comfort now against a norm that keeps relationships healthy under pressure.
examples.whatToDo: Set a norm that correction is private, calm, and aimed at behavior, and that disagreements get resolved before the day ends, because relationships stay healthy only when conflict is handled with care and promptly.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues are locked in a tense argument, and one keeps restating her position louder. A mediator says the fastest way to cool it is counterintuitive. What is it?
choices: Have a senior person declare who is right, since a clear ruling is the only thing that ends an argument.
Make the upset person feel genuinely heard first, since most conflict eases once someone feels understood rather than agreed with.
Tell them both to drop it and move on, because unresolved arguments rarely matter much in the long run.
questions.explanation: People usually want to be heard more than they want to be agreed with, so acknowledgment eases conflict faster than a verdict. Feeling understood, not winning, is what de-escalates.

questions.prompt: A manager prides herself on giving everyone the exact same blunt feedback, calling it fairness, yet several strong people seem to shut down after her reviews. What best explains it?
choices: Her people are simply too sensitive, so she should keep the identical blunt delivery and let them adjust.
The feedback content must be wrong, since delivery style has no real effect on whether a message lands.
The same message must be packaged differently per person, so an identical blunt delivery fails the ones who need it framed gently.
questions.explanation: Each person has a preferred way of receiving correction. One blunt script for everyone is not fairness; it lands for some and shuts down others, which is why the strong people withdraw.

questions.prompt: Two leaders deadlock over a decision, and the room pushes them to vote a winner. You want the healthier resolution. Which move fits?
choices: Reject the win-or-lose frame and search for a creative third option both can genuinely accept.
Hold the vote and let the majority decide, since a clear loser is the price of any real decision.
Postpone indefinitely, because a disagreement left alone usually dissolves before it matters.
questions.explanation: When two people deadlock, inventing a custom solution both can accept beats declaring a winner. A shared resolution preserves the relationship that a win-or-lose vote would damage.

questions.prompt: Your team gets plenty of correction and almost no praise. You want to rebalance the two levers of managing people. Which adjustment fits?
choices: Lead with praise in public as the primary lever, since praise is affirmation and people earn correction once they feel valued.
Keep correction as the dominant lever, because too much praise tends to make people complacent and quietly lower their own standards.
Drop both praise and criticism, since the best managers stay silent and simply let the results speak for themselves.
questions.explanation: Praise and criticism are the two levers, and praise is the more important: it is affirmation, while criticism is investment. Leading with public praise is what makes correction land as care.

questions.prompt: A leader reacts defensively whenever anyone questions a decision, and lately no one raises concerns at all. A peer says her own reactions caused the silence. How should you evaluate that?
choices: Disagree, since a leader has every right to defend her decisions and that cannot discourage real feedback.
Disagree, because quiet teams are simply content, and the absence of complaints is a sign of good morale.
Agree: reacting badly to criticism teaches people to stop bringing it, so staying receptive is part of the job.
questions.explanation: Defensiveness trains a team to withhold feedback, and then problems surface too late. Staying genuinely open to criticism is what keeps the information flowing, so the peer is right.

questions.prompt: A manager plans to deliver a tough correction by joking about the mistake in the team meeting to soften it. Why might that backfire?
choices: It will not backfire, since humor in public is the gentlest possible way to deliver any criticism.
Public, sarcastic correction humiliates rather than helps; correction belongs in private, calm, and aimed at the behavior.
The only problem is the joke was not funny enough, so a better punchline would fix the delivery.
questions.explanation: Correction belongs in private, without emotion, and aimed at the behavior, not the person. Sarcasm in public humiliates and teaches people to fear feedback rather than learn from it.

questions.prompt: A colleague says, 'Skipping a needed correction to keep the peace is a kindness.' How should you assess that against the idea that criticism is investment?
choices: Push back: withholding correction is a failure to invest in someone, so skipping it abandons them rather than being kind.
Agree, since avoiding hard conversations is usually the most considerate and respectful thing a manager can do for someone.
Agree, because correcting people rarely changes their behavior and mostly just strains the working relationship.
questions.explanation: Criticism is investment; you only bother to correct someone you believe in. Refusing to correct is not kindness but neglect, so skipping it to keep the peace actually shortchanges the person.

questions.prompt: You are setting feedback norms for a new team and want relationships to stay healthy under stress. What is the strongest design?
choices: Let people air grievances whenever and however they arise, since spontaneity is what keeps a team honest.
Correct in private and calmly, praise in public, and resolve disagreements before the day ends rather than letting them harden.
Route all conflict through you alone, so teammates rarely have to give each other difficult feedback directly.
questions.explanation: Healthy relationships run on simple disciplines done consistently: private calm correction, public praise, and not letting disputes harden overnight. Those norms hold a team together under pressure.

questions.prompt: You manage two strong people who keep clashing and avoiding each other. You want one habit that repairs the relationship. What is the best move?
choices: Separate them permanently, since two people who clash can rarely work together again productively.
Pick a winner in their disputes each time, because a clear authority is what keeps strong personalities in line.
Coach them to hear each other out and settle disagreements before leaving, so resentment never gets to harden overnight.
questions.explanation: Most friction eases when people feel heard, and disagreements left to harden overnight curdle. Coaching them to listen and resolve before the day ends rebuilds the relationship the clashes erode.

cardFronts.card01: Beyond getting your point across, what must you give a person first to ease a conflict?
cardFronts.card02: What does a team that has stopped bringing you problems reveal about how you take feedback?
cardFronts.card03: Why does tuning correction to each person transfer from one partnership to any team?
cardFronts.card04: What is the most common way leaders mistake one blunt script for honesty?
cardFronts.card05: What single question helps a manager coach better criticism and praise?
cardFronts.card06: Strong relationships sound simple. What makes a team actually practice the hard parts under pressure?

coreSkill: Make people feel genuinely heard before pressing your point, and tune correction to how each person best receives it. Keep criticism private, calm, and aimed at behavior, give praise generously in public, resolve disputes before the day ends, and stay receptive when criticized, because the simple relationship moves are what hold a team together under pressure.

ifThenContexts.1: A story about resolving one conflict creatively becomes admired but never repeated.
ifThenContexts.3: One person feeling truly heard raises the trust of the whole room.
